propagated to the API Server to host at `/config`, because it takes in a
point to the baseCfg. Point the API server to this same pointer and
handle having a shared mutex between the API server and target allocator
for accessing it.

The key logic change is to have API Server also point to the baseCfg:

```
promCfgLock := &sync.RWMutex{}
	apiServerCfg := cfg.APIServer.Get()
	var apiServerManager *apiserver.Manager
	if apiServerCfg != nil {
		apiServerManager = apiserver.NewManager(
			set,
			apiServerCfg,
			&baseCfg,
			registry,
			registerer,
			promCfgLock,
		)
	}

	pr := &pReceiver{
		cfg:          cfg,
		consumer:     next,
		settings:     set,
		configLoaded: make(chan struct{}),
		registerer:   registerer,
		registry:     registry,
		targetAllocatorManager: targetallocator.NewManager(
			set,
			cfg.TargetAllocator.Get(),
			&baseCfg,
			promCfgLock,
		),
		apiServerManager: apiServerManager,
	}
	return pr, nil
}
```

Also, move `apiserver` to internal folder to separate from
`metrics_receiver.go` main file and have parity with the`
targetallocator` design.

fix (exporter/fileexporter): Path Traversal via Windows Backslashes in Grouping File Exporter (#49195)

## Description
Fixes a path traversal vulnerability in the grouping file exporter on
Windows. When `group_by` is enabled, Windows backslashes (`\`) were not
normalized by Go's Unix-oriented `path` package, allowing directory
traversal sequences (e.g., `..\..\`) to bypass prefix containment
checks. This PR uses `filepath.ToSlash` to normalize separators on
Windows before performing containment checks, while preserving behavior
on Unix systems.


## Testing
- Added regression unit tests to `TestFullPath` using Windows-style
separators (`..\\`).
- Verified all tests pass successfully in `exporter/fileexporter`.


- 1. On Unix/Linux/macOS: filepath.Separator is /. The function is a
no-op (returns immediately). Literal backslashes (\) remain untouched,
preserving valid Unix filenames containing backslashes.


- 2. On Windows: filepath.Separator is \. The function replaces all
backslashes with /, normalizing the path segment.


- 2. Downstream APIs on Windows fully support forward slashes
Go's file APIs (os.OpenFile, os.MkdirAll, etc.) natively convert / to \
internally on Windows before calling the low-level Windows APIs.
Therefore, keeping paths with forward slashes / internally is fully
compatible on Windows and will not cause any downstream issues.




Closes #49194

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>twmb/franz-go (github.com/twmb/franz-go)</summary>

###
[`v1.21.4`](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v1214)

[Compare
Source](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/compare/v1.21.3...v1.21.4)

\===

This release is a "large" (many commits) release that has many small or
hard to encounter bugs fixed. I pointed Claude's Fable at this repo and
ran some audit rounds while available and thankfully got through the
highest
value audit rounds before Fable was removed.

For once, I will not be describing every bug fixed nor calling out every
relevant commit. Instead, if you are curious, look at
[#​1348](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/pull/1348).
Some worthwhile
description is below.

Three important bug fixes to call out:

- In transactional exactly-once consuming, a `SetOffsets` seek (which
happens
during `GroupTransactSession.End` after an aborted transaction) could be
undone by a concurrent offset load (via a background list or epoch load)
that
completed slightly later. This could happen when the client discovers a
partition leader moved while you are aborting, which could result in
missed
  records.

- Consuming with `read_committed` against a broker that returns a
partition's
  aborted-transaction list out of offset order could surface aborted,
rolled-back records as if they were committed. Apache Kafka always
returns
them in order so this was never observed there, but Redpanda does not
(when
an aborted transaction is still in memory and an earlier one is already
on
  disk). The list is now sorted client-side, matching the Java client,
  librdkafka, and Sarama.

- `GroupTransactSession.End` no longer reports a successful commit when
the
broker answers `EndTxn` with `UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR` (seen from Redpanda
in
some older versions). Previously the consumer's offsets were advanced
past a
transaction that may have aborted; now the commit is reported as failing
  and the session rewinds for reprocessing.

Beyond those, by area:

- Many transaction-path fixes for coordinator churn and KIP-890 part 2
that
would have resulted in not-working (hard client fail) or hung
transactions:
  `InitProducerID` retries `CONCURRENT_TRANSACTIONS` when taking over a
crashed producer's transaction, retriable producer-id load failures are
no
longer treated as fatal, KIP-890p2 is opted into only when the
negotiated
versions actually support it (fixing spurious `INVALID_TXN_STATE` on
4.0+
clusters running older semantics), a transaction whose every produce
failed
now aborts instead of hanging until the transaction timeout, and a
failed
`AddPartitionsToTxn` no longer drops partitions added by an earlier
request.

- `GzipCompression().WithLevel(...)` was completely broken and would
panic.

- More KIP-848 (next-gen consumer group) robustness fixes under
coordinator
  and leader churn.

- Stale consumer-group member rejoining fixes: a member that rejoins
claiming a
partition at an old generation no longer panics the group leader or
causes
  two members to consume the same partition. Malformed member metadata,
duplicate member ids, and negative claimed partitions in a join are now
rejected or sanitized rather than mis-balancing or panicking the leader.

- Metadata and topic recreation: a stale per-broker metadata view that
  momentarily omits a just-added partition (the window right after
`CreatePartitions`) no longer fails buffered producer records or leaves
a
newly assigned consumer / share partition silently unconsumed; both heal
  once metadata catches up.

- Share consumer: fetch errors are now classified like the classic
consumer
(retriable errors stripped, a metadata refresh triggered to heal a
leader
  move, top-level errors backed off) instead of stalling for up to
`MetadataMaxAge` or hot-looping, and leader-move migrations are tracked
so
  that leaving or closing cannot strand un-acked records.

- SASL: KIP-368 re-authentication no longer races the connection's other
reader, which could corrupt pipelined traffic on brokers that set a
session
lifetime (e.g. AWS MSK IAM); requests now park and replay across a
re-auth.
The Azure Event Hubs ApiVersions reset retry no longer leaks the
abandoned
  connection or silently downgrades it to v0.

- KIP-714 client telemetry: the terminating push is now actually
delivered on
`Close`, the `.rate` and `.avg` rollups are computed correctly (they
were
constant / wrong before), and an unsupported user-metric attribute no
longer
corrupts the OTLP payload (which had disabled metrics for the rest of
the
  client's life).

- Smaller consumer fixes: overlapping manual `CommitOffsets` no longer
reopen
autocommit early (which could rewind the committed offset), a conformant
  `UNDEFINED_EPOCH_OFFSET` epoch response no longer raises a false
  `ErrDataLoss`, and `Fetches.EachTopic` now preserves `TopicID` across
multi-broker responses (it was zero whenever more than one broker
replied,
  i.e. normally).

- `RecordReader` / `RecordFormatter` no longer panic on truncated or
malformed
layouts, accept `\xNN` escapes for bytes above 0x7f, and reject layouts
that
  would read nothing and loop forever.

- `WithPools`: decompression no longer produces garbage when a pool
hands back
a non-zero-length sized slice, and pooled slices are no longer leaked
for
  batches that keep no records (e.g. aborted-transaction data under
  `read_committed`).

- Other producer fixes: `EnsureProduceConnectionIsOpen` dials the right
broker
for filtered ids and no longer breaks an `acks=0` connection, the
adaptive
`LeastBackupPartitioner` now actually picks the least-backed-up
partition,
and producing during or after `Close` fails cleanly instead of hanging a
  later `Flush`.

- A broad set of guards against malformed or hostile broker responses
that
could previously panic the fetcher, hot-loop, or mis-consume: negative
or
oversized record counts and batch lengths, decompression bombs,
duplicate or
omitted partitions, negative offsets, and unexpected top-level fetch
errors.
The client is also more resilient when its own API contracts are
violated
  (e.g. `AllowRebalance` called while a poll is in flight).

</details>

[receiver/github] capture datapoint timestamp per repository (#48500)

#### Description

The scraper captured `now` once at the top of `scrape()` and reused it
when recording metrics for every repository.

Move the `now` capture inside each per-repository goroutine so each
repository's datapoints reflect when the receiver actually observed that
repository. The org-level `vcs.repository.count` still uses the
synchronously-captured outer timestamp.

To keep the test deterministic, the clock source is exposed as a `now
func() time.Time` field on `githubScraper`, defaulting to `time.Now`.
The new `TestScrapeCapturesTimestampPerRepository` injects a monotonic
clock and asserts that org-level and per-repository datapoints land at
distinct timestamps.

#### Link to tracking issue
Fixes #48497

[receiver/oracledb] Add redo log metrics (#49062)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description

The Oracle DB receiver scrapes `v$sysstat` with `SELECT * FROM
v$sysstat`, which returns all system-statistics rows. However, the
scraper only processes a subset of those rows in its `switch` block and
silently discards the rest -- including every redo-log statistic. This
PR surfaces **8 discarded redo rows** as **6 new opt-in metrics** under
the `oracledb.redo.*` namespace, giving operators visibility into redo
write latency, redo throughput, and redo-log sizing pressure -- the
foundation of Oracle's durability and recovery story (the equivalent of
PostgreSQL's WAL).

Because the data is already being fetched, the implementation is purely
additive Go code:
- **No new SQL queries**
- **No new database round-trips**
- **Zero additional load on the Oracle instance**

Related statistics are consolidated under a single metric name with an
OTel attribute rather than mapping each flat statistic to its own metric
name, following the receiver's existing attributed-metric convention.
The redo-pipeline timing statistics share one metric
(`oracledb.redo.time`) differentiated by the `oracledb.redo.type`
attribute; the redo space requests and buffer-allocation retries each
share one metric (`oracledb.redo.requests` / `oracledb.redo.retries`)
differentiated by a `oracledb.redo.request.type` /
`oracledb.redo.retry.type` attribute; and the write-direction counters
reuse the existing `disk.io.direction` attribute (introduced for
`oracledb.physical_io.*`).

This PR adds 6 new opt-in metrics (disabled by default, stability:
development):

* `oracledb.redo.time` -- Time spent in each phase of the redo pipeline.
Attribute: `oracledb.redo.type` (write|log_space_wait|sync). Covers
`v$sysstat`: `redo write time`, `redo log space wait time`, `redo synch
time` (the raw centisecond value is divided by 100 in the scraper).
* `oracledb.redo.size` -- Amount of redo generated. No attributes.
Covers `v$sysstat`: `redo size`.
* `oracledb.redo.operations` -- Number of redo I/O operations.
Attribute: `disk.io.direction` (write). Covers `v$sysstat`: `redo
writes`.
* `oracledb.redo.blocks` -- Number of redo blocks moved between the redo
log and storage. Attribute: `disk.io.direction` (write). Covers
`v$sysstat`: `redo blocks written`.
* `oracledb.redo.requests` -- Number of times a process requested space
in the redo log buffer and had to wait. Attribute:
`oracledb.redo.request.type` (log_space). Covers `v$sysstat`: `redo log
space requests`.
* `oracledb.redo.retries` -- Number of times a process waited and
retried to allocate space in the redo buffer. Attribute:
`oracledb.redo.retry.type` (buffer_allocation). Covers `v$sysstat`:
`redo buffer allocation retries`.

`oracledb.redo.time` is emitted as a `Sum` with
`aggregation_temporality: cumulative`, `monotonic: true`, value type
`double`, unit `s`. The other five are emitted as `Sum` with
`aggregation_temporality: cumulative`, `monotonic: true`, value type
`int`. Per-metric units: `s` (`oracledb.redo.time`); `By`
(`oracledb.redo.size`); `{operation}` (`oracledb.redo.operations`);
`{block}` (`oracledb.redo.blocks`); `{request}`
(`oracledb.redo.requests`); `{retry}` (`oracledb.redo.retries`).

`oracledb.redo.time` reports seconds (`s`) rather than the raw `cs`
(centisecond) units that Oracle exposes via `v$sysstat`. The scraper
divides the raw value by 100 before recording, matching the conversion
already in place for the existing `oracledb.cpu_time` metric.

The new attributes `oracledb.redo.type`, `oracledb.redo.request.type`,
and `oracledb.redo.retry.type` use dotted-namespaced receiver-scoped
keys, as no OTel semantic-convention attribute covers Oracle's
redo-pipeline phases or space-request/retry kinds.
`oracledb.redo.operations` and `oracledb.redo.blocks` reuse the existing
`disk.io.direction` attribute (currently `write`), which also leaves
room for a future read counterpart without a schema change.

The metric set covers the redo statistics present on currently-supported
Oracle (12c+); statistics that were removed in 12c (e.g. `redo writer
latching time`) or that are not exposed by `v$sysstat` are intentionally
excluded.

These metrics can be enabled in the collector configuration:

```yaml
receivers:
  oracledb:
    datasource: "oracle://user:password@host:1521/service"
    metrics:
      oracledb.redo.time:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.redo.size:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.redo.operations:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.redo.blocks:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.redo.requests:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.redo.retries:
        enabled: true
 ```

[receiver/oracledb] Add buffer cache and DBWR metrics (#49063)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description

The Oracle DB receiver scrapes `v$sysstat` with `SELECT * FROM
v$sysstat`, which returns all system-statistics rows. However, the
scraper only processes a subset of those rows in its `switch` block and
silently discards the rest -- including every buffer-cache and Database
Writer (DBWR) statistic. This PR surfaces **7 discarded `v$sysstat`
statistics** as **6 new opt-in metrics** under the
`oracledb.buffer_cache.*`, `oracledb.buffer.*`, and
`oracledb.checkpoint.*` namespaces, giving operators visibility into
buffer-cache activity, free-buffer pressure, and whether DBWR keeps up
with the workload.

Because the data is already being fetched, the implementation is purely
additive Go code:
- **No new SQL queries**
- **No new database round-trips**
- **Zero additional load on the Oracle instance**

The two related free-buffer-inspection statistics are consolidated under
a single metric (`oracledb.buffer.inspected`) differentiated by the
`oracledb.buffer.state` attribute, following the receiver's existing
attributed-metric convention; the remaining metrics are standalone
counters.

This PR adds 6 new opt-in metrics (disabled by default, stability:
development):
* `oracledb.buffer_cache.block.changes` -- Number of changes that were
part of an update or delete operation made to blocks in the buffer
cache. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `db block changes`.
* `oracledb.buffer_cache.block.gets` -- Number of current-mode block
gets satisfied from the buffer cache. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`:
`db block gets from cache`. Distinct from the existing
`oracledb.db_block_gets` metric (`v$sysstat` `db block gets`), which
counts all current-mode block gets requested regardless of where they
are satisfied.
* `oracledb.buffer.requests` -- Number of times a reusable or free
buffer was requested to create or load a block. No attributes. Covers
`v$sysstat`: `free buffer requested`.
* `oracledb.buffer.inspected` -- Number of buffers inspected from the
end of the LRU queue while a process searched for a reusable buffer, by
state. Attribute: `oracledb.buffer.state` (free|dirty). Covers
`v$sysstat`: `free buffer inspected` (state=free) and `dirty buffers
inspected` (state=dirty).
* `oracledb.checkpoint.buffers` -- Number of buffers written by the
Database Writer (DBWR) for checkpoints. No attributes. Covers
`v$sysstat`: `DBWR checkpoint buffers written`.
* `oracledb.checkpoint.completed` -- Number of checkpoints completed by
the Database Writer (DBWR). No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `DBWR
checkpoints`.

All 6 metrics are emitted as `Sum` with `aggregation_temporality:
cumulative`, `monotonic: true`, value type `int`. Per-metric units:
`{change}` (`oracledb.buffer_cache.block.changes`); `{get}`
(`oracledb.buffer_cache.block.gets`); `{request}`
(`oracledb.buffer.requests`); `{buffer}` (`oracledb.buffer.inspected`,
`oracledb.checkpoint.buffers`); `{checkpoint}`
(`oracledb.checkpoint.completed`).

The new attribute `oracledb.buffer.state` (enum: free, dirty) uses a
dotted-namespaced receiver-scoped key; no OTel semantic-convention
attribute covers Oracle's LRU buffer-inspection states.

Note: the free-buffer activity is sourced from Oracle's current `free
buffer requested` / `free buffer inspected` / `dirty buffers inspected`
statistics. The older `DBWR make free requests` / `DBWR free buffers
found` / `DBWR buffers scanned` statistics that these replaced are not
present on Oracle 12c+ (verified against the Oracle 19c Statistics
Descriptions and a live 19c instance), so they are intentionally not
used.

These metrics can be enabled in the collector configuration:

```yaml
receivers:
  oracledb:
    datasource: "oracle://user:password@host:1521/service"
    metrics:
      oracledb.buffer_cache.block.changes:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.buffer_cache.block.gets:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.buffer.requests:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.buffer.inspected:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.checkpoint.buffers:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.checkpoint.completed:
        enabled: true
```

[oracledbreceiver] Add workload analysis metrics (#48837)

#### Description

The Oracle DB receiver currently scrapes `v$sysstat` with `SELECT * FROM
v$sysstat`, which returns all system statistics rows. However, the
scraper only processes a small subset of those rows in its `switch`
block and silently discards the rest. PR #48335 surfaced the first batch
of discarded rows as OTLP-attributed metrics (physical I/O bytes,
requests, cache writes, SQL*Net throughput). This PR continues that work
by surfacing **26 additional discarded rows** as **14 new opt-in
metrics** — covering table/index scans, enqueue (lock) operations, LOB
I/O, SQL parse time, sort operations, cursor activity, user/recursive
calls, and DB time. Together they give operators a workload-analysis
view of an Oracle instance suitable for capacity planning and SQL/lock
contention investigation.

Because the data is already being fetched, the implementation is purely
additive Go code:
- **No new SQL queries**
- **No new database round-trips**
- **Zero additional load on the Oracle instance**

This PR adds 14 new opt-in metrics (disabled by default, stability:
development):

* `oracledb.scan.count` — Total count of scan operations. Attributes:
`oracledb.scan.type` (`table` | `index_fast_full`) and
`oracledb.scan.mode` (`direct_read` | `full` | `long_tables` |
`rowid_ranges`). Covers `v$sysstat`: `table scans (direct read | long
tables | rowid ranges)` and `index fast full scans (direct read | full |
rowid ranges)`.
* `oracledb.scan.table.rows` — Total number of rows returned by
full-table scans. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `table scan rows
gotten`.
* `oracledb.enqueue.operations` — Total count of enqueue (lock)
operations. Attribute: `oracledb.enqueue.type` (`conversions` |
`releases` | `requests` | `timeouts` | `waits`). Covers `v$sysstat`:
`enqueue conversions | releases | requests | timeouts | waits`.
* `oracledb.lob.operations` — Total count of LOB (large object) I/O
operations. Attribute: `disk.io.direction` (`read` | `write`). Covers
`v$sysstat`: `lob reads`, `lob writes`.
* `oracledb.parse.cpu.time` — Total CPU time spent on SQL parsing, in
seconds. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `parse time cpu` (raw
centiseconds divided by 100).
* `oracledb.parse.elapsed.time` — Total wall-clock time spent on SQL
parsing, in seconds. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `parse time
elapsed` (raw centiseconds divided by 100).
* `oracledb.sort.operations` — Total count of sort operations.
Attribute: `oracledb.sort.type` (`disk` | `memory`). Covers `v$sysstat`:
`sorts (disk)`, `sorts (memory)`.
* `oracledb.sort.rows` — Total number of rows sorted across all sort
operations. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `sorts (rows)`.
* `oracledb.cursor.cache.hits` — Total count of session cursor cache
hits, where an existing cached cursor is reused to avoid a soft parse.
No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `session cursor cache hits`.
* `oracledb.cursor.cache.size` — Number of cursors currently held in the
session cursor cache. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `session cursor
cache count`.
* `oracledb.cursor.open` — Number of currently open cursors in the
Oracle instance. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`: `opened cursors
current`.
* `oracledb.call.count` — Total count of calls issued to the database.
Attribute: `oracledb.call.type` (`user` | `recursive`). Covers
`v$sysstat`: `user calls`, `recursive calls`.
* `oracledb.call.recursive.cpu.time` — Total CPU time spent on recursive
(internal) calls, in seconds. No attributes. Covers `v$sysstat`:
`recursive cpu usage` (raw centiseconds divided by 100).
* `oracledb.db.time` — Total wall-clock time spent in database calls, in
seconds. Attribute: `oracledb.session.type` (`foreground`). Covers
`v$sysstat`: `DB time` (raw centiseconds divided by 100).

Counters are emitted as `Sum` with `aggregation_temporality: cumulative`
and `monotonic: true`. `oracledb.cursor.cache.size` and
`oracledb.cursor.open` are emitted as `Gauge` — point-in-time values
that can decrease as well as increase (e.g. the cursor cache shrinks
when sessions terminate). Per-metric units: `s`
(`oracledb.parse.cpu.time`, `oracledb.parse.elapsed.time`,
`oracledb.call.recursive.cpu.time`, `oracledb.db.time`); `{operation}`
(`oracledb.scan.count`, `oracledb.enqueue.operations`,
`oracledb.lob.operations`, `oracledb.sort.operations`); `{row}`
(`oracledb.scan.table.rows`, `oracledb.sort.rows`); `{hit}`
(`oracledb.cursor.cache.hits`); `{cursor}`
(`oracledb.cursor.cache.size`, `oracledb.cursor.open`); `{call}`
(`oracledb.call.count`).

The four time-based metrics report seconds (`s`) rather than the raw
`cs` (centiseconds) Oracle exposes via `v$sysstat`; the scraper divides
by 100 before recording, matching the conversion already used by
`oracledb.cpu_time`.

Attribute naming follows OTel semantic conventions where they exist or
were established in PR #48335 (`disk.io.direction`), and uses dotted,
receiver-scoped keys for the new enums (`oracledb.scan.type`,
`oracledb.scan.mode`, `oracledb.enqueue.type`, `oracledb.sort.type`,
`oracledb.call.type`, `oracledb.session.type`) so future fields stay
collision-free with future semconv additions. On `oracledb.scan.count`,
`oracledb.scan.type` identifies what was scanned (table vs. index fast
full) and `oracledb.scan.mode` identifies how Oracle executed it. On
`oracledb.call.count`, `oracledb.call.type` distinguishes user calls
from Oracle's internal recursive calls.

These metrics can be enabled in the collector configuration:

```yaml
receivers:
  oracledb:
    datasource: "oracle://user:password@host:1521/service"
    metrics:
      oracledb.scan.count:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.scan.table.rows:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.enqueue.operations:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.lob.operations:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.parse.cpu.time:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.parse.elapsed.time:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.sort.operations:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.sort.rows:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.cursor.cache.hits:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.cursor.cache.size:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.cursor.open:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.call.count:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.call.recursive.cpu.time:
        enabled: true
      oracledb.db.time:
        enabled: true
```

The main goal of adding those new functions are logging purposes, and

[receiver/postgresqlreceiver] Add Postgres blocking session attributes to db.server.query_sample (#48953)

Fixes #49028

## Summary

- Adds PostgreSQL blocking session detection to `db.server.query_sample`
events in the `postgresqlreceiver`
- Introduces 7 new attributes, all consolidated under the
`postgresql.blocking.*` hierarchy:
- `postgresql.blocking.pids` — array of PIDs blocking this session (from
`pg_blocking_pids()`)
- `postgresql.blocking.start_time` — UTC timestamp (RFC3339) of when the
current lock wait began (from `pg_locks.waitstart`)
- `postgresql.blocking.wait_duration` — whole seconds the session has
been waiting for a lock
- `postgresql.blocking.lock.mode` — lock mode being requested (e.g.
RowExclusiveLock, AccessExclusiveLock)
- `postgresql.blocking.lock.type` — lock resource type being waited on
(e.g. relation, transactionid, tuple)
- `postgresql.blocking.lock.relation` — name of the relation (table)
being waited on
- `postgresql.blocking.transaction.start_time` — UTC timestamp (RFC3339)
when the current transaction started
- Uses `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...LIMIT 1)` on `pg_locks` to prevent row
duplication from advisory locks having multiple `granted = FALSE`
entries per session
- Idle-in-transaction blocker sessions (sessions not actively running
but holding locks) are captured via a `pg_blocking_pids` subquery
exception in the WHERE clause

## Design Decisions

- **`pg_locks.waitstart` for blocking start time**: this gives the exact
timestamp when the lock wait began. `waitstart` is set once when the
process enters `ProcSleep()` and is stable for the full duration of the
wait — it is not affected by blockers joining or leaving. It is cleared
only when the lock is finally granted.
- **LATERAL LIMIT 1 join**: A session waiting on an advisory lock can
have multiple `granted = FALSE` rows in `pg_locks`. Plain `LEFT JOIN`
would fan out and produce duplicate log records per sample. `LATERAL
(...LIMIT 1)` picks the earliest ungranted lock entry per session.
- **transaction.start_time from xact_start**:
`pg_stat_activity.xact_start` represents when the current transaction
started — it predates the lock contention itself and is useful for
understanding total transaction age independently of when blocking
began.
- **All attributes always emitted**: Empty string / 0 when the session
is not blocked (OTel convention: no post-emit attribute removal).
- **blocking.pids as array string**: `pg_blocking_pids()` natively
returns a PostgreSQL array (e.g. `{5121,5122,5188}`). Stored as string
to match how other receivers handle multi-value identifiers.

## Test plan

- Unit tests pass with race detector
- Lint clean
- Golden file tests updated for blocked and non-blocked sessions
- Template rendering test validates full SQL shape with LATERAL join
- SQL mock tests updated to match new LATERAL join query shape

## Known Limitations

- **blocking.pids is AND semantics**: All listed PIDs must release
before the blocked session can proceed — this differs from Oracle/SQL
Server which track a single direct blocker.
- **Sub-second waits show as 0**: `blocking.wait_duration` truncates to
whole seconds via `::BIGINT`. Use `blocking.start_time` being non-empty
as the authoritative signal that a session is actively blocked.

[processor/dynamic_sampling] add new dynamic sampling processor for adaptive trace sampling (#48899)

Closes #48898

## Overview

Adds `processor/dynamic_sampling`, a tail-based sampling processor that
dispatches each trace to the first matching rule's sampler, emits
`ot=th:<hex>` on every sampled span via `pkg/sampling`, and records the
matched rule name as a span attribute. Design rationale and the case for
a separate processor are in the linked issue and the [processor
README](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/blob/mike/dynamicsamplingprocessor/processor/dynamicsamplingprocessor/README.md).

This PR is a proof-of-concept submitted alongside the proposal issue to
demonstrate the full design. If maintainers prefer, it can be broken up
to follow `docs/new-components.md` (initial scaffold PR + follow-ups per
sampler).

## What's included

- Five sampler types: `always_sample`, `deterministic`, `ema_dynamic`,
`ema_throughput`, `windowed_throughput`. The three adaptive samplers
wrap [`dynsampler-go`](https://github.com/honeycombio/dynsampler-go).
- First-match rule evaluation with `(conditions, sampler)` pairs;
matched sampler's decision is final.
- `ot=th:<hex>` emission compatible with the `spanmetrics` connector's
adjusted count feature.
- Rule attribution via the `otelcol.processor.dynamic_sampling.rule`
span attribute.
- Trace accumulation with `trace_timeout`, `decision_delay`,
`num_traces` eviction.
- Two-tier LRU decision cache for late-arriving spans.
- Internal telemetry: active-trace gauge, per-rule sampled/dropped
counters, per-rule sample-rate histogram, eviction counter.

## Dependencies

One new third-party dependency:

| Module | Version | Licence | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|
[`github.com/honeycombio/dynsampler-go`](https://github.com/honeycombio/dynsampler-go)
| v0.6.4 | Apache-2.0 | EMA-based adaptive sampling algorithms |

`dynsampler-go` is actively maintained by Honeycomb and used in
production by Refinery at scale.

## Test plan

- Unit tests covering config validation, rule matching, condition
parsing, sampler types, trace accumulation, sampling decisions,
TraceState encoding, rule attribution, deterministic distribution, and
LRU eviction
- Race detector clean (`go test -race ./...`)
- Linter clean (`make lint`)
- `make checkapi`, `make checkdoc`, `make checkmetadata`, `make
chlog-validate` all pass
- `otelcontribcol` builds with the new processor wired in

fix(exporter/awsxray): use local service name for Consumer local root segments (#47568)

## Description

Fixes #43432.

After PR #42633, Consumer spans that are local roots are promoted to
X-Ray **Segments** (rather than just subsegments). However, the segment
naming logic in `MakeSegment` still treated Consumer spans like
dependency spans (using `aws.remote.service` / operation name), while
Server segments already used `aws.local.service` /
`resource.service.name`.

### Root cause

Two gaps in `MakeSegment` (both in `segment.go`):

1. **`aws.local.service` check (line 361)** — only guarded by
`SpanKindServer`, so Consumer local root spans never used this attribute
for naming.
2. **`resource.service.name` fallback (line 425)** — also only for
`SpanKindServer`, so Consumer local root spans fell through to the span
(operation) name.

### Fix

Extend both checks to also cover `SpanKindConsumer &&
isLocalRoot(span)`:

```go
// Before
if span.Kind() == ptrace.SpanKindServer {

// After  
if span.Kind() == ptrace.SpanKindServer || (span.Kind() == ptrace.SpanKindConsumer && isLocalRoot(span)) {
```

The dependency **subsegment** produced alongside the service segment is
unaffected: `MakeDependencySubsegmentForLocalRootDependencySpan`
explicitly overrides the name to `aws.remote.service` after calling
`MakeSegment`, so the subsegment name remains correct.

### Tests

- Existing `TestLocalRootConsumer` and
`TestLocalRootConsumerAWSNamespace` continue to pass.
- New `TestLocalRootConsumerUsesResourceServiceName`: Consumer local
root span **without** `aws.local.service` attribute — service segment
name must be `resource.service.name` (`"signup_aggregator"`), not the
operation name (`"destination operation"`).

fix(pkg/stanza): avoid emitting partial log after read error in tcp O… (#49199)

OneLogPerPacket mode

Assisted-by: Claude

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description
When `one_log_per_packet: true` is set on the tcp input operator, if the
connection read fails mid-copy (e.g. connection reset), the error is
logged and the partially-read buffer is still processed and emitted as a
complete log entry. That's bad: you get corrupted log entries that look
legitimate but aren't.

So, to fix I added an early return immediately after the error is
logged. Now partial/corrupt data is discarded instead of being
processed.

```go
if err != nil {
    i.Logger().Error("IO copy net connection buffer error", zap.Error(err))
    return
}
```

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.

#### Description

The per-sample conversion loop re-allocated the `valuesByProfile` outer
slice on every OTLP sample even though its length is invariant. Each
`pprofSample.Value` also grew from `nil` via repeated appends despite
the final size being known upfront, and the locations slice was built
without a pre-allocated backing array even though the stack depth is
available before the loop. Fix this by hoisting the `valuesByProfile`
allocation before the loop, pre-allocating `pprofSample.Value` with
`make([]int64, numProfiles)`, and pre-allocating locations with the
stack's location count as capacity.

[chore] [exporter/googlemanagedprometheus] Fix invalid filter processor syntax in README example (#49425)

### Context
Resolves #49414 
The troubleshooting section of the `googlemanagedprometheus` exporter
README contained a syntactically invalid example for configuring the
`filter` processor. It incorrectly used a YAML list for `metrics`
instead of a map, causing startup failures when users copy-pasted the
config.

### Changes
- Updated the `filter` processor example to use the modern OTTL
`metric_conditions` format.
- Replaced the deprecated `metrics:` map syntax with
`metric_conditions:` and explicitly used `metric.name != ...`.

### Verification
- [x] Verified that the new configuration matches the current
`filterprocessor` documentation and OTTL standards.

[internal/coreinternal] Exclude AIX from CGO strptime validation tests (#49485)

#### Description
AIX's `struct tm` does not have `tm_gmtoff` (a glibc/BSD extension), so
`strptime_cgo_testlib.go` fails to compile on AIX/ppc64.

```
timeutils/strptime_cgo_testlib.go:34:36: tm.tm_gmtoff undefined (type _Ctype_struct_tm has no field or method tm_gmtoff)
timeutils/strptime_cgo_testlib.go:48:3: unknown field tm_gmtoff in struct literal of type _Ctype_struct_tm (typecheck)
 ```

https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/psfa/7.1.0?topic=representations-support-struct-tm-temporal-structures
> The API uses the strict implementation of struct tm which does not contain the additional fields tm_zone and tm_gmtoff

This PR excludes `internal/coreinternal/timeutils/strptime_cgo_test.go` and `internal/coreinternal/timeutils/strptime_cgo_testlib.go` on AIX to fix the compilation errors.

Introduced by https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/pull/48112.

#### Testing
Validated that it fixed the compilation error on AIX.

[chore][internal/coreinternal] Fix compile error and skip test in strptime_cgo_test.go when using old glibc (#49516)

#### Description
Similarly to
https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/pull/49485,
when using glibc versions older than 2.19, `struct tm` doesn't have a
`tm_gmtoff` field by default, resulting in compilation errors.

```
Error:
    # github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/internal/coreinternal/timeutils
/var/cache/dd/go/pkg/mod/github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/internal/coreinternal@v0.155.0/timeutils/strptime_cgo_testlib.go:34:36: tm.tm_gmtoff undefined (type _Ctype_struct_tm has no field or method tm_gmtoff)
/var/cache/dd/go/pkg/mod/github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/internal/coreinternal@v0.155.0/timeutils/strptime_cgo_testlib.go:48:3: unknown field tm_gmtoff in struct literal of type _Ctype_struct_tm
```

Defining `_BSD_SOURCE` (the ancestor of `_DEFAULT_SOURCE`, already
defined here) fixes the compilation issue.

Running the test still fails with old glibc or when using musl libc,
because they don't support some of the `%z` formats used in those tests
(`[+-]HH` vs `[+-]HHMM` vs `[+-]HH:MM` vs `Z`), so I also added a check
to skip the test when not using a recent glibc version.

Musl:
```
Error:        Received unexpected error:
              strptime failed to parse the whole string
Test:         TestParseStrptimeCgo/iso-8601-utc/2007-04-05T12:30:46+00:00
```

Glibc 2.17:
```
Error:        Received unexpected error:
              strptime failed to parse the whole string
Test:         TestParseStrptimeCgo/iso-8601-utc/2007-04-05T12:30:46Z

Error:        Received unexpected error:
              strptime failed to parse: remainder ":00"
Test:         TestParseStrptimeCgo/iso-8601-hst/2007-04-05T06:07:08-10:00
```

#### Testing
Validated on Linux using a recent glibc (compiles, runs, and passes), an
old glibc (skipped), and musl (skipped).

### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>twmb/franz-go (github.com/twmb/franz-go)</summary>

###
[`v1.21.5`](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v1215)

[Compare
Source](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/compare/v1.21.4...v1.21.5)

\===

Three bug fixes:

- Fixed a nil-pointer panic when building a group `OffsetFetch`: if the
group
  was assigned a topic that was no longer in the client's tracked set --
reachable when a topic is purged from consuming while still assigned,
for
example `PurgeTopicsFromConsuming` overlapping `AddConsumeTopics`, or
the
  automatic regex missing-topic purge -- `loadTopic` returned nil and
dereferencing it for the topic ID crashed the client. The topic ID is
now
only set when the topic is known. Thanks
[@​iwittkau](https://redirect.github.com/iwittkau)!

- Fixed a data race on a coordinator's cached node ID. When a broker
disconnected while a `FindCoordinator` load for that broker was still in
flight, `deleteStaleCoordinatorsByNode` could read the in-flight load's
`node` field before the loading goroutine published it (via closing the
  load's wait channel), which `go test -race` flagged. The node read now
  happens only after the load has been observed as complete. Thanks

[@​nikolauspschuetz](https://redirect.github.com/nikolauspschuetz)!

- A share partition that was listed in a ShareFetch only to carry a
piggybacked acknowledgement -- for a cursor that was revoked, paused, or
migrated to a new leader after its records were drained -- was added to
the
broker's share session but never tracked client-side, so it could never
be
  forgotten. The broker would re-acquire and redeliver that partition's
  records indefinitely while the client discarded them ("broker returned
  partition ... we did not ask for"), spinning the share fetch loop. The
client now tracks every partition it sends, matching the broker's
session
  bookkeeping.

#### Relevant commits

-
[`ab185e42`](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/commit/ab185e42)
**bugfix** kgo: add nil check when loading topics in groupConsumer
(thanks [@​iwittkau](https://redirect.github.com/iwittkau)!)
-
[`aca084ed`](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/commit/aca084ed)
**bugfix** kgo: fix data race on coordinatorLoad.node (thanks
[@​nikolauspschuetz](https://redirect.github.com/nikolauspschuetz)!)
-
[`754bc349`](https://redirect.github.com/twmb/franz-go/commit/754bc349)
**bugfix** kgo: forget piggyback-only partitions from the share session

</details>

[pkg/stanza/fileconsumer] Fix gzip fingerprint generation when file offset is non-zero (#49474)

## Description

Fixes #49473.

This PR fixes gzip fingerprint generation when the provided file
descriptor is positioned at a non-zero offset.

Previously, `NewFromFile` created a `gzip.NewReader` using the current
file position. If the file had already been seeked away from the
beginning of the file, fingerprint generation could fail with:

```text
gzip: invalid header
```

This change temporarily seeks to the beginning of the file before
creating the gzip reader and restores the original file offset
afterwards.

A regression test has also been added to verify that fingerprint
generation succeeds regardless of the current file offset while
preserving the original file position.

## Testing

```bash
go test ./pkg/stanza/fileconsumer/internal/fingerprint
```

The added regression test (`TestNewFromFileGzipOffset`) verifies:

- Fingerprint generation succeeds when the file is already positioned at
a non-zero offset.
- The generated fingerprint matches the fingerprint generated from the
beginning of the file.
- The original file offset is restored after fingerprint generation.

Three bug fixes:

- Fixed a nil-pointer panic when building a group `OffsetFetch`: if the
group
  was assigned a topic that was no longer in the client's tracked set --
reachable when a topic is purged from consuming while still assigned,
for
example `PurgeTopicsFromConsuming` overlapping `AddConsumeTopics`, or
the
  automatic regex missing-topic purge -- `loadTopic` returned nil and
dereferencing it for the topic ID crashed the client. The topic ID is
now
only set when the topic is known. Thanks

- Fixed a data race on a coordinator's cached node ID. When a broker
disconnected while a `FindCoordinator` load for that broker was still in
flight, `deleteStaleCoordinatorsByNode` could read the in-flight load's
`node` field before the loading goroutine published it (via closing the
  load's wait channel), which `go test -race` flagged. The node read now
  happens only after the load has been observed as complete. Thanks

[@​nikolauspschuetz](https://redirect.github.com/nikolauspschuetz)!

- A share partition that was listed in a ShareFetch only to carry a
piggybacked acknowledgement -- for a cursor that was revoked, paused, or
migrated to a new leader after its records were drained -- was added to
the
broker's share session but never tracked client-side, so it could never
be
  forgotten. The broker would re-acquire and redeliver that partition's
  records indefinitely while the client discarded them ("broker returned
  partition ... we did not ask for"), spinning the share fetch loop. The
client now tracks every partition it sends, matching the broker's
session
  bookkeeping.

[internal/sqlquery] close sql.Rows to release driver connection (#49463)

QueryRows called db.QueryContext but never closed the returned
*sql.Rows, so any early return (ColumnTypes error, scanner error, or
context cancellation mid-iteration) held the driver connection until GC.
On drivers that allocate per-connection buffers (e.g. go-mssqldb's 64
KiB TDS buffer), this manifested as steady RSS growth under long-running
scrapes across all sqlquery-consuming receivers (sqlserver, postgresql,
mysql, oracledb, sqlquery).

  * db_client.go: defer sqlRows.Close() after the QueryContext check.
* db_wrappers.go: add Close() error to the rows interface and delegate
from rowsWrapper to sql.Rows.Close().
* db_client_test.go: no-op Close() on fakeRows to satisfy the widened
interface.

Fixes #49462

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description

Fixes a connection leak in the shared sqlquery helper: `QueryRows` in
`db_client.go` called `db.QueryContext` but never closed the returned
`*sql.Rows`, so any early return (an error, or the caller stopping
iteration) held the underlying driver connection until GC finalized
the Rows object. On go-mssqldb specifically, each unclosed Rows also
pinned a TDS response buffer, which surfaced as steady RSS growth
under long-running scrapes rather than just connection-pool
exhaustion.

The fix defers `sqlRows.Close()` immediately after the `QueryContext`
error check, and threads `Close() error` through the `rows`
abstraction so both the real `rowsWrapper` and test doubles satisfy
the interface.

Fix units to comply with UCUM standard (#49453)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description

Fixes units on `metadata.yaml` files to conform to the [UCUM
specification](https://ucum.org/).

The intent is to add validation to mdatagen, see
open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/pull/15530.

<details>
<summary>LLM-generated per-change table with UCUM spec
justification</summary>

| Component(s) | Was | Now | Reason & UCUM reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `receiver/apachesparkreceiver` | `bytes` | `By` | The byte symbol is
`By`. See [§48 *Units used in information technology*, Table
22](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-48) (byte, c/s = `By`). |
| `receiver/haproxyreceiver`, `receiver/memcachedreceiver` | `by` | `By`
| Wrong case. The byte symbol is `By`. See [§48 *Units used in
information technology*, Table 22](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-48) (byte,
c/s = `By`) and [§3 *Character set*](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-3). |
| `receiver/apachesparkreceiver` | `mb` | `MBy` | `mb` is not valid (`m`
is the *milli* prefix and `b` is not a unit). Megabyte is the `M`
(*mega*) prefix applied to `By`. See [§27 *Prefixes*, Table
1](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-27) (`M` = mega) and [§48 Table
22](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-48) (byte, metric = yes). |
| `receiver/sqlserverreceiver` (`"KB"`), `receiver/nsxtreceiver`,
`receiver/splunkenterprisereceiver` (`KBy`) | `KB` / `KBy` | `kBy` | The
kilo prefix is lowercase `k`; uppercase `K` is not a UCUM prefix.
Kilobyte is `k` + `By`. See [§27 *Prefixes*, Table
1](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-27) (`k` = kilo) and [§48 Table
22](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-48) (byte `By`). |
| `receiver/chronyreceiver` | `"ppm"` | `"[ppm]"` | Parts per million is
a dimensionless unit written with square brackets as `[ppm]`. See [§29
*Dimensionless units*, Table 3](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-29) (`[ppm]`
= `10*-6`) and [§5 *Square brackets*](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-5). |
| `receiver/chronyreceiver` | `seconds` | `s` | The second is a base
unit with symbol `s`. See [§28 *Base units*, Table
2](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-28) (second = `s`). |
| `receiver/mongodbreceiver` (`"microseconds"`),
`processor/tailsamplingprocessor` (`µs`) | `microseconds` / `µs` | `us`
| `microseconds` is not a symbol, and the micro sign `µ` is not ASCII,
so it is outside the UCUM character set. UCUM uses `u` for the *micro*
prefix, giving `us`. See [§3 *Character
set*](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-3) (ASCII only) and [§27 *Prefixes*,

ASCII, so it is outside the UCUM character set. The degree-Celsius
symbol is `Cel`. See [§3 *Character set*](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-3)
(ASCII only) and [§30 *SI units*, Table
4](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-30) (degree Celsius = `Cel`). |
| `receiver/nginxreceiver` | `connections`, `requests` |
`"{connections}"`, `"{requests}"` | These are counts of things, not
physical units. UCUM expresses such labels as annotations in curly
braces; an annotation with no leading symbol implies the unity `1`. They
are quoted so YAML treats them as strings rather than flow mappings. See
[§6 *Curly braces*](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-6). |
| `receiver/sqlserverreceiver` | `“{errors}”`, `“{deadlocks}/s”`,

`"{deadlocks}/s"`, `"{transactions}/s"`, … | Typographic quotes (`“ ”`)
wrapped the values. These quotes are not ASCII, so they are outside the
UCUM character set and became part of the string. Removing them leaves
valid curly-brace annotations, re-quoted with plain double quotes for
YAML. See [§3 *Character set*](https://ucum.org/ucum#para-3) and [§6

[receiver/postgresql] Adding postgresql.query.conflicts metric (#49303)

#### Description
Add a new optional metric `postgresql.query.conflicts` sourced from
`pg_stat_database_conflicts`, reporting the number of queries canceled
due to recovery
conflicts on standby servers. The five conflict counters (tablespace,
lock, snapshot,
bufferpin, deadlock) are consolidated into a single metric with a `type`
attribute to
avoid metric explosion.

The metric is a cumulative monotonic Sum, consistent with the receiver's
other counters,
and is disabled by default. Conflicts only occur on standby servers, so
it reads zero on
primaries; the query is only issued when the metric is enabled.

Adds a dedicated client query (`getDatabaseConflicts`), scraper wiring,
unit tests for the
client and scraper, and regenerated mdatagen output.

#### Testing
- Added unit tests:
- `TestGetDatabaseConflicts` in `client_test.go`, using `sqlmock` to
verify the
`pg_stat_database_conflicts` query and row scanning for both
all-databases and
    database-filtered cases.
- Updated scraper tests to enable the metric and regenerated the golden
files
(`testdata/scraper/otel/expected.yaml`, `expected_schemaattr.yaml`), so
the new
metric and its `type` attribute datapoints are asserted end-to-end
through the
    MetricsBuilder.
  - Regenerated `internal/metadata` tests via `mdatagen`.
- Manually verified against a live cluster: stood up a PostgreSQL
primary + streaming
standby (tuned with `max_standby_streaming_delay=0` and
`hot_standby_feedback=off`)
and generated recovery conflicts (snapshot and lock conflicts) on the
standby. With
the metric enabled, the collector emitted non-zero
`postgresql.query.conflicts`
datapoints broken down by `type` on the standby, and zero on the
primary, as expected.

#### Documentation
The metric is self-documented through `metadata.yaml`; running
`mdatagen` regenerates
`documentation.md` with the new `postgresql.query.conflicts` entry
(description, unit
`{query}`, type, and the `type` attribute and its enum values). 
A changelog entry is added under
`.chloggen/postgresql-database-conflicts-metric.yaml`.

[receiver/hostmetrics/cpu] Make logical CPU attribute opt-in (#49162)

Marks the host_metrics CPU scraper `cpu` attribute opt-in for
`system.cpu.time`, `system.cpu.utilization`, so the default output is
aggregated by state.

To restore the previous per-logical-CPU output, re-enable `cpu`
attribute by applying the following config:
  ```yaml
  receivers:
    hostmetrics:
      scrapers:
        cpu:
          metrics:
            system.cpu.time:
              attributes: [cpu, state]
            system.cpu.utilization:
              attributes: [cpu, state]
```

Fixes #49161

[receiver/hostmetrics] Enable system.cpu.logical.count metric by default (#49325)

Enables `system.cpu.logical.count` by default in the hostmetrics CPU
scraper. With #49162 making the per-CPU `cpu` attribute opt-in for CPU
time and utilization, default CPU metrics should still preserve logical
CPU cardinality. This metric is important host information and is
recommended by the System CPU semantic conventions.

To restore the previous behavior, disable the new metric by applying the
following config:

```yaml
receivers:
  hostmetrics:
    scrapers:
      cpu:
        metrics:
          system.cpu.logical.count:
            enabled: false
```

Marked as breaking because it changes the default emitted telemetry.

#### Testing
To test we can use a real Elasticsearch and force a mapping conflict
to get a document level 400.

##### 1. Start Elasticsearch

```bash
docker run \
  --rm \
  --name es \
  -p 9200:9200 \
  -e discovery.type=single-node \
  -e ELASTIC_PASSWORD=changeme \
  -d \
  docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:9.4.2
```

Then check the logs and wait until Elasticsearch is ready, you can test
the connection and credentials:

```bash
# silent, accept the self-signed cert
curl -sk -u elastic:changeme https://localhost:9200
```

Once Elasticsearch is up and running you'll have a response like:
```json
{
  "name" : "f0ac801af371",
  "cluster_name" : "docker-cluster",
  "cluster_uuid" : "YqaIF-9JTJy7VlAud-wVbA",
  "version" : {
    "number" : "9.4.2",
    "build_flavor" : "default",
    "build_type" : "docker",
    "build_hash" : "c402c2b36d90eae29c0182f86bd9050fd0b746cc",
    "build_date" : "2026-05-25T22:10:36.017759931Z",
    "build_snapshot" : false,
    "lucene_version" : "10.4.0",
    "minimum_wire_compatibility_version" : "8.19.0",
    "minimum_index_compatibility_version" : "8.0.0"
  },
  "tagline" : "You Know, for Search"
}
```

##### 2. Create an Index with explicit mappings

Documents with incorrect types will be rejected.

```bash
curl -sk -u elastic:changeme -XPUT https://localhost:9200/otel-doc-retry-test \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "mappings": {
      "properties": {
        "bad_field": { "type": "long" }
      }
    }
  }'
```

The response should be:
```json
{"acknowledged":true,"shards_acknowledged":true,"index":"otel-doc-retry-test"}
```

##### 3. Build the test Collector

```bash
make otelcontribcol
```

##### 4. Start the Collector

Create `/tmp/otel-doc-retry.yaml`:

```yaml
receivers:
  filelog:
    include: [/tmp/test.log]
    start_at: beginning
    poll_interval: 2s
    operators:
      - type: json_parser
        parse_to: body

exporters:
  elasticsearch:
    endpoints: [https://localhost:9200]
    user: elastic
    password: changeme
    tls:
      insecure_skip_verify: true

    logs_index: otel-doc-retry-test
    mapping:
      allowed_modes: [bodymap]

    retry:
      enabled: true
      max_retries: 2
      initial_interval: 100ms
      max_interval: 100ms
      retry_on_status: []
      retry_on_document_status: [400]

    telemetry:
      log_response_body: true
      log_failed_docs_input: true

    sending_queue:
      enabled: true
      batch:
        min_size: 0
        flush_timeout: 1s
        sizer: bytes

service:
  telemetry:
    logs:
      level: debug
      output_paths:
        - /tmp/otelcol-logs.log
        - stdout
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [filelog]
      exporters: [elasticsearch]
```

Run the collector:

```bash
# The collector will log to /tmp/otelcol-logs.log and stdout
# Adjust the binary name to your platform
./bin/otelcontribcol_linux_amd64 --config /tmp/otel-doc-retry.yaml
```

In another shell:

```bash
echo '{"message":"retry me","bad_field":"not-a-long"}' >> /tmp/test.log
```

With `retry_on_document_status: [400]` and `max_retries: 2`, expect 3
`_bulk` requests: initial attempt and 2 document retries.

```bash
grep '_bulk' /tmp/otelcol-logs.log
# To coult the bulk requests
grep -c '_bulk' /tmp/otelcol-logs.log
```

The document still fails after retries, so Elasticsearch count should
remain `0`:

```bash
curl -sk -u elastic:changeme https://localhost:9200/otel-doc-retry-test/_count
```

[receiver/oracledb]: Add SGA component memory metrics from V$SGAINFO (#48542)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### What's the problem?
The Oracle DB receiver currently has no metrics sourced from V$SGAINFO.
The System Global Area (SGA) is Oracle's primary shared memory region —
it holds the buffer cache, shared pool, redo log buffer, and other
critical components that directly determine database throughput and
query performance.

- **No memory breakdown:** The SGA contains several independently
tunable components (Buffer
Cache, Shared Pool, Large Pool, Redo Buffers). When Oracle degrades due
to memory pressure,
operators cannot determine which component is undersized without
manually querying the
    database.
- **Cannot detect misconfiguration:** Oracle's `db_cache_size` and
`shared_pool_size` parameters
control SGA component sizes. When misconfigured — too small for the
workload — Oracle evicts
cached data aggressively, causing hard parses, physical I/O spikes, and
query latency
degradation. Without per-component SGA sizes, these misconfigurations
are invisible to the
    collector.
- **Hit ratio metrics lack size context:** The receiver already exposes
`oracledb.buffer_cache.utilization` (hit ratio), but a low hit ratio on
a 256MB buffer cache
means something very different than the same ratio on a 16GB cache.
Without the absolute size,
the hit ratio metric lacks the context needed for actionable alerting.
- **No correlation with OS memory:** The receiver exposes total physical
memory via
`system.memory.limit` (from V$OSSTAT). Without SGA component sizes,
operators cannot determine
what fraction of available memory Oracle is using or whether SGA growth
is approaching the
    physical memory ceiling.

  #### What does this add?
One new opt-in metric (disabled by default, stability: development),
sourced from a single query against V$SGAINFO:

  **oracledb.sga.usage** (gauge int, unit By)
Size in bytes of each component of the System Global Area (SGA) as
reported by V$SGAINFO.
Named `.usage` per OTel instrument naming conventions — each component
value represents an amount
currently allocated out of the total SGA. Broken down by the
`oracledb.sga.component` attribute
(e.g. `Buffer Cache Size`, `Shared Pool Size`, `Large Pool Size`, `Redo
Buffers`, `Fixed SGA
Size`, `Maximum SGA Size`). A single attributed gauge replaces what
would otherwise be 8+
separate metrics, following the standard OTel pattern for
named-component breakdowns (analogous
  to `system.memory.usage` with `state` attribute).

The only additional privilege required is `GRANT SELECT ON V_$SGAINFO TO
<username>`, documented in the README.

[tailsamplingprocessor] Fix race in iter() that delays config updates (#48889)

[processor/tailsamplingprocessor] Fix race condition in iter() causing
config updates to be applied after trace evaluation

Issue: TestDropLargeTraces in processor/tailsamplingprocessor fails
intermittently on CI. The test verifies that raising
MaximumTraceSizeBytes via SetMaximumTraceSizeBytes is correctly applied
to subsequent trace data—but CI reports traces_dropped_too_large = 2
(instead of 1) and allSampledTraces having 1 item instead of 2.

Approach: I traced the concurrent execution paths in iter() and
identified that Go's select statement is non-deterministic. When
SetMaximumTraceSizeBytes queues an update on newTraceSizeChan at the
same time as ConsumeTraces queues a batch on workChan, the runtime may
process the work batch first—applying the old (low) size limit and
incorrectly dropping the trace. The fix is to eagerly drain
config-update channels at the start of the workChan branch.

[receiver/postgresql] Explicitly ignoring tables with AccessExclusiveLock to prevent receiver from stalling (#49352)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description
Fixes a bug in which the receiver completely stalls and doesn't emit any
metric if the `database` has a table which has an active
`AccessExclusiveLock` lock being held by some process / connection.

The culprit is the query in `getDatabaseTableMetrics()` function as also
mentioned in the issue.
The "fix" now explicitly ignores the tables which an active
`AccessExclusiveLock`. Since the scraper runs in cycles, this should be
okay because the table will get scraped once the lock doesn't exists
anymore. Moreoever, this also protects the receiver in case an orphan
process has an exclusive lock and there is not lock or statement based
timeout set in the PostgreSQL instance.

Query before -
```sql
SELECT schemaname as schema, relname AS table,
	n_live_tup AS live,
	n_dead_tup AS dead,
	n_tup_ins AS ins,
	n_tup_upd AS upd,
	n_tup_del AS del,
	n_tup_hot_upd AS hot_upd,
	seq_scan AS seq_scans,
	pg_relation_size(relid) AS table_size,
	vacuum_count
FROM pg_stat_user_tables;
```

Query after -
```sql
SELECT
    s.schemaname AS schema,
    s.relname AS table,
    s.n_live_tup AS live,
    s.n_dead_tup AS dead,
    s.n_tup_ins AS ins,
    s.n_tup_upd AS upd,
    s.n_tup_del AS del,
    s.n_tup_hot_upd AS hot_upd,
    s.seq_scan AS seq_scans,
    pg_relation_size(s.relid) AS table_size,
    s.vacuum_count
FROM pg_stat_user_tables s
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT DISTINCT relation
    FROM pg_locks
    WHERE locktype = 'relation'
      AND mode = 'AccessExclusiveLock'
      AND granted = true
) l ON s.relid = l.relation
WHERE l.relation IS NULL;
```

I applied similar fix in `getIndexStats()`'s query since it can also get
blocked if a `REINDEX` is happening on the index. However, this has
smaller impact compared to the change done in
`getDatabaseTableMetrics()` since I don't think REINDEX is that
frequent.

[exporter/file] Fix orphaned lumberjack backup files after migration to timberjack (#47694)

#### Description

After the migration from `natefinch/lumberjack` to `DeRuina/timberjack`
(#45900), rotated backup files created by the previous lumberjack-based
exporter used a different filename pattern (`data-<timestamp>.jsonl`)
that timberjack does not recognize. Timberjack's cleanup logic requires
a `-<reason>` suffix (e.g. `data-<timestamp>-size.jsonl`). It silently
ignores files without it, causing them to be excluded from `max_backups`
and `max_days` enforcement and accumulate indefinitely on disk,
eventually filling the volume.

On startup, the file exporter now scans the log directory and renames
any lumberjack-format backup files to the timberjack convention by
appending `-size` (the only rotation reason lumberjack supported). After
renaming, Timberjack owns its full lifecycle, `max_backups` and
`max_days` are enforced normally, including during runtime rotations.

No new configuration option was added because the affected files are
already invisible to Timberjack and effectively leaked, so all users
upgrading from the lumberjack-based version are impacted. An opt-in flag
would mean most users never benefit from the fix and remain at risk of
disk-full conditions. The rename is conservative and becomes a no-op
once all legacy files have been migrated.

#### Link to tracking issue
Fixes #47674

#### Testing

Unit tests added covering:
- Rename of lumberjack-format files to timberjack convention with
`-size` suffix
- Timberjack recognizes and enforces `max_days` on renamed files
(integration with real `timberjack.Logger`)
- All timberjack filename variants left untouched (reasons `size`,
`time`, custom; compression suffixes `.gz`, `.zst`; append-after-ext
naming)

[receiver/k8sobjectsreceiver] Fix panic and data race during leader re-acquisition (#49602)

### Context
When the receiver loses leadership, `stopWatches()` closes the channels
in `stopperChanList` but leaves them in the slice. When the receiver
re-acquires leadership, `start()` appends new stop channels to the same
slice. When stopping again, the receiver attempts to close
already-closed channels, resulting in a panic. Furthermore, `start()`
mutated `stopperChanList` without holding the mutex `kr.mu`, causing a
data race with `stopWatches()`.

### Changes
- Reset `stopperChanList` to `nil` in `stopWatches()` under lock.
- Acquire `kr.mu` lock in `start()` before appending to
`stopperChanList`.
- Call `Shutdown` at the end of `TestReceiverWithLeaderElection` to
ensure leader changes and shutdowns are fully verified.

### Verification
- Ran `go test -v ./...` in the `receiver/k8sobjectsreceiver` directory.
All tests passed.

[processor/spanpruning] Add bytes metrics (#49008)

## Add serialized bytes metrics to span pruning processor

### Description

This PR adds opt-in serialized byte-size telemetry to the span pruning
processor, enabling users to measure the data-volume impact of pruning
rather than just span counts. It builds on the existing core pruning,
parent recursion, and aggregation metrics.

### Changes

**New feature: Bytes Metrics**

Span-count metrics show how many spans were pruned, but not how much
serialized data that saved. This feature serializes trace data with
`ptrace.ProtoMarshaler` and reports the byte sizes before and after
pruning, for both the full batch and the matched subset of traces.

Visibility is provided through four counter metrics (unit `By`,
monotonic, disabled by default):

- `processor_spanpruning_bytes_received` - full batch size before
pruning
- `processor_spanpruning_bytes_processed_input` - matched subset size
before pruning
- `processor_spanpruning_bytes_processed_output` - matched subset size
after pruning
- `processor_spanpruning_bytes_emitted` - full batch size after pruning

Implementation notes:

- The feature is opt-in because measuring it serializes each batch (full
batch plus the matched subset before/after pruning), which adds CPU
overhead and is expensive for large batches.
- `spanInfo` now tracks its `ResourceSpans` (in addition to
`ScopeSpans`) so the new `getBytes` helper can reconstruct the original
RS/SS hierarchy when sizing a subset of traces.
- A `matchedTraces` set is wired into `processTraces` as a stand-in for
future OTTL `conditions` filtering. Until conditions are supported in
contrib, every trace is treated as matched, so `bytes_processed_input ==
bytes_received` and `bytes_processed_output == bytes_emitted`. The split
is in place so the matched-subset metrics become meaningful once
condition filtering lands.

**Configuration options**:
```yaml
processors:
  spanpruning:
    # Enable measurement of serialized trace sizes before and after pruning.
    # Serializes each batch (full batch plus matched subset) and is expensive
    # for large batches.
    enable_bytes_metrics: true   # default: false
```

When `enable_bytes_metrics` is `false`, behavior is unchanged and no
bytes metrics are emitted.

### Testing

- Processor tests asserting the bytes metrics are recorded only when
enabled and absent when disabled
- Tests verifying `bytes_processed_input == bytes_received` and
`bytes_processed_output == bytes_emitted` when no conditions are
configured
- Tests verifying input/output bytes match when no aggregation runs, and
that all counters drop when pruning reduces serialized size
- Updated the generated telemetry tests (`metadatatest`)

### Documentation

Updated README with the `enable_bytes_metrics` option, the four new
metrics, and a "Byte metrics semantics" section explaining valid
comparisons now and the forward-looking behavior once `conditions`
support is added (including the case where aggregation summaries can
make `bytes_processed_output` exceed `bytes_processed_input`); added the
four counters to `metadata.yaml` and regenerated the telemetry code.

[receiver/webhookeventreceiver] Make webhookeventreceiver to support HMAC signature authentication (#47189)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code

#### Description
HMAC Signature Verification

The receiver supports HMAC-SHA256 hex digest signature verification,
which is used by webhook providers like GitHub and Fingerprint to ensure
payload integrity and authenticity. When configured, the receiver reads
the raw request body, computes the HMAC-SHA256 digest using the shared
secret, and compares it with the signature in the specified header.
Requests with missing or invalid signatures are rejected with HTTP 401
Unauthorized.

##### GitHub webhook example

```yaml
receivers:
    webhookevent:
        endpoint: localhost:8088
        path: "/github/webhooks"
        hmac_signature:
            secret: "your-github-webhook-secret"
            header: "X-Hub-Signature-256"
            prefix: "sha256="
```

##### Fingerprint webhook example

```yaml
receivers:
    webhookevent:
        endpoint: localhost:8088
        path: "/fingerprint/webhooks"
        hmac_signature:
            secret: "your-fingerprint-webhook-secret"
            header: "fpjs-event-signature"
            prefix: "v1="
```

[extension/azureencodingextension] fix NDJSON detection for CRLF line endings (#49608)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### Description

- Azure Blob Storage blobs that use Windows-style line endings `(\r\n)`
(as example of Application Gateway diagnostic logs written directly to
Storage Accounts) were not being recognised as NDJSON.
- The detection code in `helpers.go` were looking for `\n` and then the
byte immediately before, expecting a `}`. But with CRLF the byte is
`\r`, so the check was failing, causing logs to not be ingested.
- Logs in the collector would show `"Unable to detect JSON format"`.
- The current check changes `DetectWrapperFormat()` inside `helpers.go`
to also accept `}\r` before `\n` as a valid NDJSON line ending.

<!--Describe what testing was performed and which tests were added.-->
#### Testing

- `helpers_test.go`: Two new cases added to the existing
`TestDetectorWrapperFormat` table test:
-- NDJSON with CRLF line endings -> correctly detected as `FormatNDJSON`
-- A single JSON object with a trailing `\r\n` -> also correctly
detected as `FormatNDJSON`

### Description

Preparatory refactor split from #48663 to keep that PR reviewable.

This PR introduces **no behavioral changes**, it only refactors code
required for the `informer` adoption on k8s_objects receiver.

initialization before returning (cache sync), which can time out or

change was necessary to surface failures from the new one.

#### Summary

This release updates the default lychee version from `v0.23.0` to
`v0.24.2`.

The main reason for this release is compatibility with the new lychee
`0.24.x` release artifacts. Starting with lychee `v0.24.0`, the archive
layout changed, and the `lychee` binary may now be packaged inside a
subdirectory. `lychee-action` now detects that layout automatically, so
users can upgrade without changing their workflows.

If you use:

```yaml
uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2
```

you will get the new version once the floating `v2` tag has been
updated. If you pin exact versions, update to:

```yaml
uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2.9.0
```

#### What’s new from lychee `v0.24.x`

##### Better diagnostics

lychee now reports line and column numbers for detected links. This
makes broken link reports easier to act on, especially in larger
documentation sites or generated reports.

##### Text fragment checking

lychee can now check URL text fragments, such as links containing
`#:~:text=...`. This helps catch links that point to a valid page but no
longer points to the intended highlighted text.

##### Sitemap support

lychee can now read `sitemap.xml` inputs. This is useful for checking
published websites or generated documentation sites where the sitemap is
the easiest source of URLs to validate.

##### JUnit output

lychee now supports JUnit output. This makes it easier to integrate link
checking results with CI systems and test reporting tools that
understand JUnit XML.

##### Redirect and remap visibility

lychee can now show redirects and remaps more clearly. This helps
explain why a URL was checked as a different final URL and makes
debugging link-checking behavior easier.

##### Multiple config files

lychee now supports multiple configuration files and expanded config
handling. This is useful for repositories that split documentation,
website, or package-specific link-checking settings.

##### Timeout handling

lychee can now accept timeouts explicitly. This gives users more control
over how strict their link checks should be for flaky or slow endpoints.

#### Fixes and reliability improvements

##### Fixed lychee `0.24.x` archive compatibility

`lychee-action` now handles the new lychee release archive layout by
detecting whether the `lychee` binary is inside a subdirectory.

This fixes compatibility with lychee `0.24.x`.

##### More stable installation path

The action now installs lychee into `$RUNNER_TEMP/lychee/bin` instead of
`$HOME`.

This avoids failures on runners where `$HOME` differs between composite
action steps. In those environments, the action could add one directory
to `PATH` but install the binary somewhere else, causing `lychee:
command not found`.

##### Safer automatic lychee version updates

The workflow that checks for new lychee releases now guards against
`null` release versions before creating update PRs. This prevents
invalid automated PRs such as “Update lycheeVersion to null”.

##### Dependency updates

- Updated `actions/checkout` from `v6` to `v7`
- Updated `actions/cache` from `v5` to `v6`

[receiver/oracledb]: Add OS-level metrics from V$OSSTAT (#48459)

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.
Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.-->
#### What's the problem?                                       
The Oracle DB receiver currently has no metrics sourced from V$OSSTAT.
This creates a critical blind spot when diagnosing Oracle performance
issues:
                                                            
- **No OS resource baseline:** When an Oracle instance slows down,
operators cannot determine from the collector alone whether the cause is
a database-level issue (slow queries, lock contention) or an OS-level
resource problem (CPU saturation, memory pressure). Without OS context,
every incident requires manual cross-referencing with infrastructure
dashboards - slowing down root cause analysis.
- **CPU count unknown:** Every CPU-related metric in the receiver is
uninterpretable without knowing how many CPUs Oracle has available. A
load of 4.0 is an emergency on a 2-CPU instance but entirely normal on a
16-CPU one. Without NUM_CPUS, customers cannot write meaningful CPU
saturation alerts.
- **Load average not tracked:** OS load average is the earliest warning
signal of resource saturation - it rises before CPU utilization hits
100%, before query latency degrades, and before users notice slowdowns.
Without it, customers can only react to outages rather than prevent
them.
- **Total memory not exposed:** Oracle's SGA and PGA are sized relative
to available physical memory. When memory pressure builds - from a
growing workload, a memory leak, or an undersized instance - Oracle
begins paging to disk, causing dramatic and hard-to-diagnose query
slowdowns. Without total memory, customers cannot detect misconfigured
memory parameters (db_cache_size, pga_aggregate_target) before they
cause degradation.

#### What does this add?
Three new opt-in metrics (disabled by default, stability: development),
all following OTel semantic conventions for naming and units:
                                                            
**oracledb.os.cpu.limit** (gauge int, unit {cpu})
Number of CPUs available to the Oracle instance as reported by the OS
(NUM_CPUS). Provides the baseline denominator for all CPU-related
metrics and alerting thresholds. Named .limit per OTel instrument naming
conventions - NUM_CPUS is a fixed constant, not a variable count.
**oracledb.os.load** (gauge double, unit 1)
Current OS load average (LOAD). Unbounded metric representing average
runnable processes - values exceeding oracledb.os.cpu.limit indicate CPU
saturation. Named freely as .load per OTel spec ("other instruments that
do not fit the standard suffixes may be named more freely") since load
average is not a [0,1] fraction and does not qualify as utilization.
                                                            
**oracledb.os.memory.limit** (gauge int, unit By)
Total physical memory in bytes (PHYSICAL_MEMORY_BYTES). Named .limit per
OTel instrument naming conventions - total physical memory is a fixed
constant, not an amount currently in use. Provides the ceiling for
Oracle memory configuration (SGA + PGA).
All three metrics are sourced from a single query against V$OSSTAT. The
only additional privilege required is GRANT SELECT ON V_$OSSTAT TO
`<username>`, documented in the README.

[loadbalancingexporter] Remove endpoint-order bias from ring construction (#49585)

#### Description
This updates the hash ring. Now, ring construction no longer depends on
the order of the resolved endpoints.

The previous implementation built the ring endpoint by endpoint and
claimed positions as it went. With many endpoints and a shared
occupied-position map, earlier endpoints got first access to scarce
positions and later endpoints were more likely to probe or lose points
entirely. That left a residual skew even after the earlier
collision-handling improvements in #41271.

This change keeps the existing 4-byte virtual node index and linear
probing, but changes how ring positions are assigned:

1. all virtual points are generated first
2. candidates are globally ordered before any assignment happens
3. collisions are resolved from that global ordering instead of endpoint
input order

The result is that the same endpoint set now produces the same ring
regardless of the order in which the endpoints are provided, and the
distribution across large backend sets is noticeably more uniform.

This also changes the defaults introduced during the investigation:

- `defaultWeight`: `100` -> `200`
- `maxPositions`: `36000` -> `131071`

`131071` was chosen deliberately. It is `2^17 - 1`, which keeps the ring
much larger than the old `36000` slot space without using an exact power
of two. During the issue investigation, powers of two behaved poorly
with the current `crc32 % maxPositions` scheme, while `131071` gave a
much better tradeoff between collision pressure, distribution quality,
and ring size cost.

<!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue.

#### Description
Adds 5 new opt-in metrics sourced from sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats
(SAMPLED mode) covering all user indexes across all databases on the
instance:

- sqlserver.index.fragmentation (gauge, %)
- sqlserver.index.page.count (gauge, {pages})
- sqlserver.index.size (gauge, By)
- sqlserver.index.page.utilization (gauge, %)
- sqlserver.index.record.count (gauge, {records})

All metrics carry db.namespace, sqlserver.schema.name,
sqlserver.object.name, and sqlserver.index.id attributes for per-index
identity. On-prem/MI uses a cursor over sys.databases with an outer
TRY/CATCH so restricted logins return partial results (accessible
databases) rather than failing the entire scrape. Azure SQL DB uses a
direct single-database branch.

All metrics are disabled by default (stability: development).

###
[`v2.8.0`](https://redirect.github.com/mongodb/mongo-go-driver/releases/tag/v2.8.0):
MongoDB Go Driver 2.8.0

[Compare
Source](https://redirect.github.com/mongodb/mongo-go-driver/compare/v2.7.0...v2.8.0)

The MongoDB Go Driver Team is pleased to release version 2.8.0 of the
official MongoDB Go Driver.

#### Release Highlights

This release supports the general availability of Queryable Encryption
string queries. The query types `prefix`, `suffix`, and `substring` are
added as generally available for MongoDB 9.0+ and libmongocrypt 1.20.0.
The query types `prefixPreview`, `suffixPreview`, and `substringPreview`
remain experimental for 8.2–8.x servers and may be removed in a future
release.

Other key facts:

This release bounds an unchecked pre-allocation in the

##### Security/robustness

The attribute decoder (`unmarshalFileStat`) allocated the
extended-attribute slice directly from the wire-supplied

could advertise a huge `extended_count` in a small packet and force a
multi-gigabyte allocation up front, crashing the process with `fatal
error: out of memory` before a single entry was parsed.
